en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who was a bearer of the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
Now begins the *Nayavīthī*, adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages.
The third chapter, titled "The Name.
The Declaration of the Chapter’s Subject Matter: In order to establish that all cognition here is indeed in accordance with its object—
The true nature of the teacher Prabhākara is now being elucidated. // 1 //

Regarding this, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: First, some of refined intellect have declared that both erroneous cognition (*bhrama*) and doubt (*sandeha*) are cognitions that do not correspond to reality (*ayathārtha*). (Verse 2)
If this cognition, "This is silver," which arises regarding a fragment of mother-of-pearl, were to be considered true to the object, then what kind of erroneous nature could it possibly possess? (3)
If even a cognition that appears as the object exactly as it exists is an error, then all means of valid cognition would consequently fall into the nature of error. (4)
If it is argued that the non-apprehension of distinction is an error, this is not so;
for such an error would follow even in deep sleep, since all distinctions are not apprehended there.
If, when a piece of land has been seized,
there should be a state of delusion, then that delusion would consist in seeing only a general form from a distance.
Moreover, if [the cognition] were a perception of things as they truly are, even a sublation would not be possible;
for a cognition that constitutes a sublation could not arise from the apprehension of a difference that was previously unknown. (7)
Furthermore, one should also consider how this [cognition] can be considered to correspond with reality;
for it determines mother-of-pearl to be silver. (8)
Silver-ness does not belong to the shell, nor does shell-ness belong to the silver;
their mutual difference is ascertained by direct perception. (9)
Now, if this [cognition] does not apprehend the mother-of-pearl as being silver, then its apprehension through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be contradicted. (10)
Furthermore, the activity of one seeking silver toward mother-of-pearl would be without basis;
for even the non-apprehension of a difference is not the cause of such activity. (11)
Furthermore, this cognition of silver does not arise for one who is blind;
therefore, it is dependent upon the sense faculty, and the sense faculty produces cognition only when it is in contact [with its object]. (12)
The sense organ, when in contact with mother-of-pearl, is capable of producing [that cognition];
therefore, by means of that very sense organ, it is apprehended here as silver. (13)
It might be thought: "Only the mother-of-pearl is apprehended by the sense organ;
that very object, through its similarity [to silver], is the cause for the recollection of silver. (14)

In this case, through a similar cognition that serves as the cause for awakening a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), there arises a memory of silver devoid of the mental representation "that" (*tad*). (15)
In this state of memory, the "that" (tad) component is fragmented due to a defect in the mind;
therefore, the claim that [memory] conforms to the senses is established otherwise and is incorrect.

Even regarding an object that has been experienced, they do not consider a cognition devoid of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of it to be memory, just like a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-bodha*).
Because it possesses co-referentiality with an object directly present before one's eyes, this is not memory;
rather, it is an erroneous apprehension of silver regarding mother-of-pearl. (18)
Furthermore, in dreams, there exists no cause whatsoever for the awakening of memory;
the same applies to the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the perception of two moons. (19)
Furthermore, how can errors such as the confusion of directions or the whirling firebrand (alātacakra) be described as being based on memory in accordance with reality? (20)
Therefore, due to defects such as those of the sense faculties, erroneous cognitions arise, perceiving the nature of an object in one way when it exists in another. (21)
Even the doubt that arises as to whether it is a post or a person—since such an object does not exist—how could that [cognition] be in accordance with reality? // 22 // 38 //
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
Here we say—whatever object appears within whatever consciousness, that alone is the knowable; for nothing else indeed is the definition of the knowable. (23)
In the cognition "this is silver," it is silver that appears; therefore, only that [silver] would be the object of knowledge, and not the mother-of-pearl, because the latter is not perceived. (24)
Therefore, the appearance of one thing as another is refuted by perception itself;
for when one thing is appearing, another does not appear. // 25 //
[Objection: But in that case, how will this appearance as silver be possible?
[Response: It is said: the fragment of mother-of-pearl is perceived devoid of its distinction [from silver]. (26)
Those specific qualities of the mother-of-pearl which are the causes for its distinction from silver are not cognized due to being overwhelmed; rather, it is its common form that is cognized. (27)
Immediately thereafter, memory arises regarding the silver; nevertheless, due to a defect in the mind, it is devoid of the reflective awareness of that [silver] as such. (28)
Since silver has been made the object [of cognition] and was not distinguished from the mother-of-pearl by memory, the appearance of silver will thus be logically established.

And as for what has been stated—that this memory is to be understood as a continuous stream—it is said so because there is no other possible way to account for it; thus, memory is to be understood here [in that manner]. (30)
For silver that is not present cannot be an object of perception;
nor can it be the domain of any other means of valid cognition, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga) and so forth. (31)

From that, the certainty arises that [the cognition] is memory by way of elimination, because its cause exists; however, this is not the case in the case of continuous streams of cognitions (dhārāvāhika-buddhi). // 32 //
The cause for grasping the collection of present sense-faculties is [the mind];
and these two—grasping and recollection—do not manifest as distinct from one another. (33)
Although, in reality, [the object] is indeed distinct from the correct cognition of silver,
nevertheless it does not appear as distinct, because of the equality of the non-apprehension of difference.

And since correct cognition of silver has as its object a single thing present before one's eyes, these two—recollection and perception—are not understood to be distinct from that [present object]. (35)
People perceive [the self] as being of a uniform nature solely through the cognition of objects that are not directly present and through the apprehension of objects that are common to others. (36)
Thus far, it has been established that there is a cognition of non-distinction;
from that very [cognition], worldly transaction proceeds in a manner identical to that [non-distinction]. (37)

And because consciousness possesses equality and because it does not perceive difference, even though it is false, it functions as if it were real due to its initiating a corresponding conventional usage. (38)

Therefore, even a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) is considered to be a benefactor (*bandhaka*) to people who are mistaken regarding the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of silver, because it prevents the occurrence of that practical application of silver which was [otherwise] about to take place. (vv.

Just as there arises a cognition of silver regarding a piece of silver that is actually present, so too does this [cognition] manifest in a similar manner due to the non-apprehension of the difference [between the object and the mental representation]. (41)
For there exists a common form belonging to both that [past object] and this [present one]; therefore, because it appears as that alone, they consider them to be identical. // 42 //
Therefore, the practical usage of identity with that [object] and the resulting activity are also justified;
and because it effects the removal of that [error], even the subverting cognition possesses the quality of being a subverter.
In this way, even in dreams, objects that exist as mere memories appear as if they were being perceived, through the loss of the aspect of having been previously experienced. (44)
For the specific characteristic of apprehension is that memory is an apprehension of what has already been apprehended;
it stands as if it were an act of apprehension by way of concealing the portion [of the object] that was already apprehended.
And in that case, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated as the cause for the awakening of latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*);
for this same hypothesis applies equally even to the theory of erroneous manifestation (*viparītakhyāti*).
Furthermore, because the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is a cause, such a cognition does not arise for one who is awake;
for even a state [of consciousness] occurs when the fruit of the causal complex of the unseen force is produced.
And in the perception of a yellow conch shell, the yellowness belonging to the bile residing in the sense organ is apprehended,
devoid of any external substance, just as heat is perceived in water.
Due to a defect in the sense organ, the whiteness of the conch is not perceived;
only the substance itself appears, devoid of its color. (49)
When a quality is perceived as depending on a substance, and a substance is perceived as requiring a quality,
the cognition of those two does not apprehend them as being unrelated.
Even when there is the appearance of truth, these two cognitions appear as equal; worldly convention is likewise similar to that,
and thus it is appropriate here as well.
As for the fact that the blackness of collyrium, even when located in the eye, is not perceived, the cause for that is the obstruction of the sense faculty by it. (52)
That circle of the eye which resembles the flax flower, and the collyrium situated therein, is that which obstructs the functioning of the fire element (tejas). // 53 //
Furthermore, when a certain ointment is applied to the eyes, the blackness [of the pupil] is not perceived due to the defect of its lack of rectitude within the circle. (54)
Even when covered on the upper part of the sense organ by bile, the visual light is not obstructed due to its transparent nature, just as it is not obstructed by glass. (55)

The light that issues forth from the eye is the perceiver; it does not reside within the sense organ itself. Its non-perception [as a substance] is due to its subtlety, just as the light of a flame is not perceived [as a distinct object].

In this way, the cognition of bitterness toward what is sweet has been explained as being devoid of bile, due to the perception of pungency and the grasping of molasses which lacks [actual] flavor. (57)
Likewise, even in the cognition of two moons, the distinct sensory light produces two separate appearances within a single cool-rayed moon. (58)
Your two cognitions do not differ; when there is duality [of objects], one merely thinks so.
Indeed, even here, as before, it is simply a case of having cognitions of different objects that are similar [in nature]. (59)
Even when there is a recollection of oneness, this delusion arises because of that [recollection];
for it is not held that delusion occurs everywhere through the loss of memory.

In the case of confusion regarding direction, error is held to arise because the capacity [of the sense organ] has not been observed, because the true nature of direction is not grasped, and because of the recollection of the true nature of another direction. (61)

In the case of a whirling firebrand, when the firebrand is rotated rapidly in all directions, the cognitions that arise without interruption are considered to be equivalent to the cognition of a wheel. (62)
However, because those cognitions are so rapid, their temporal distinction is not perceived;
therefore, the conventional usage of the term "cognition of a wheel" is appropriate even in this case.
In this very manner, the wise should infer the distinctions among causes within all types of delusions, for the sake of establishing knowledge of reality as it is. (64)
Even when there is doubt as to whether it is a post or a person, if both are remembered as being mutually exclusive, how could there be an absence of the object [in that case]? (69)
If some cognition were to arise while abandoning its object, being erroneous regarding its own referent, how could it be a cause for confidence? // 66 //

But surely, even here, there is an equal lack of confidence due to the suspicion that it might be equivalent to the cognition of non-silver; if you argue that the determination [of validity] occurs there because of the absence of defects, [we reply: 67.
This same [objection] is seen even in the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*);
alas, what a great error this is, even for the wise! (68)
If cognition were indeed fallible, upon what basis could there be confidence?
Even if cognition is fallible, that which is known [by it] remains truly existent. (69)
Is there not even ignorance that serves as the basis for the distinction between forms?
This very desire to know arises, and it too is removed by something else. (70)
Even when it is sought with effort, if that form is not seen,
then the previous cognition itself is designated as being the reality.
Furthermore, on the view that cognition does not correspond to reality, it would follow that cognition possesses a form;
for whatever form appears resides in the cognition itself. (72) 51)
There is no cause for the non-arising of a cognition that does not correspond to reality;
if you claim it is due to defects, it is not so, for defects merely obstruct the capacity of the effect to arise. (73) 52.
In cases such as *bhasmaka* (hypermetabolism), it is precisely because of the obstruction of the effect that [the cause] is considered a fault;
for indeed, the production of nutritional essence (*rasa*) is the effect of the fire residing in the stomach. (74)
It is logically established that defects act as obstacles to the apprehension of the form of an existing object; thus, delusion is a bondage consisting of non-apprehension. (75)
In order to establish that all cognitions are non-deviant with respect to their objects,
this *Nayavīthī* was composed by Śālikanātha, the knower of political science (or logic).
Miśra Śalikanātha has composed this work titled *Nayavīthī* for the benefit of the world, in accordance with the doctrine of Prabhākara. (77)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Path of Policy" (*nītipatha*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the venerable Great Mahopādhyāya Śālikanātha Miśra.
